# Engineering Criteria

The one owner of the bar code is judged and built against. Callers load it by name and apply the sections their work touches: `full-review` judges a codebase against them and owns how gaps become findings; `orchestrated-refactor` slices and `root-cause` fixes meet them for what they change; scaffolding workflows hold generated code to them. A change meets the criteria for the code it adds or changes; gaps it discovers elsewhere follow the caller's discovered-work rule: the calling skill's own handling where it has one, else the global rules' Discovered work bullet (Minimal-Code Discipline) where installed, else the consuming repository's own rule; with none, report them to the user (an unattended run, through its caller) instead of fixing them. Security handling (held findings, disclosure) belongs to the calling skill or the global rules, and items below marked as security defects follow it; otherwise a discovered security or data-exposure defect goes only to the user, never into a tracked file, commit, PR, issue or comment text until the user decides how it is fixed, whatever a repository's general discovered-work rule says.

## Principles

- Value = likelihood x impact / effort. Act on what realistically breaks, leaks, costs or slows; keep designs pragmatic: no over-engineering, gold-plating, heavy validation of unlikely edge cases or defenses against states the types, callers or framework already rule out. Input crossing a trust boundary is never speculative or an unlikely edge case.
- Baseline by default: we are creating the baseline. Unless the user or repo states a compatibility obligation (a policy, a README stating a compatibility promise to consumers, or a configured package-validation baseline version; API baseline files that only guard against accidental breaks are not one):
  - Refactoring is approved where it makes code simpler, more maintainable or more scalable: it reduces complexity or risk, never relocates it. Churn without one of those gains is not approved. Consistency with the codebase beats local elegance unless the convention is the defect.
  - Breaking code and API changes are accepted; no backward compatibility, shims, deprecation paths, legacy accommodation or code kept only for past versions.
  - Code, comments, docs and instructions describe the current design only, never its history: no "previously", "renamed from", "old" or "legacy" notes. Git holds the history; records kept as history (changelogs and release notes, handoffs, review-yield tables, dated evidence) stay.
  - Data is the exception: applied migrations stay as written; changes to persisted or in-flight data (stored rows, queued and outbox messages, caches, serialized payloads, data exchanged between this system's own components during a mixed-version rollout) or deployed schema keep it readable through new, data-preserving migrations or a reader kept until it drains, with its removal condition, and irreversible data and schema operations still need confirmation.
- Stability first: the simplest design that is correct on every reachable case and resilient wins. Clever workarounds, accommodations for unlikely cases and extra mechanisms are built only when explicitly requested or required by the criteria below, apart from an unavoidable, scoped and commented third-party mitigation; security, accessibility, data-loss and trust-boundary handling are never cut for simplicity.
- Standards first: framework-native and well-known patterns before custom abstractions; a new dependency must clearly earn its place.
- License stability: prefer the platform and its first-party libraries, then open-source components under an open license, meaning an OSI-approved permissive (such as MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC or PostgreSQL) or weak-copyleft (such as MPL-2.0) one, governed by a foundation or a broad contributor base. This covers the project's build and runtime dependencies, self-hosted servers included; not developer tooling installed on machines or separately billed managed services.
  - New dependencies: one already under a source-available, commercial or otherwise more restrictive license, or one that already moved to such a license, is a dependency change the user approves first. One whose single vendor controls the copyright (or holds a CLA that lets it relicense) and sells a commercial edition is used only when no foundation- or community-governed alternative fits the need, with that reason recorded in the change.
  - Existing dependencies: one still on its last open version stays there and takes security fixes released under an open license; a fix released only under the new license goes to the user as a security finding. One already on a post-move version, or licensed by the user on purpose, is reported to the user once (not when the repo's dependency or license notes record it as deliberate; when the user confirms it is, add that note) and downgraded only with the user's approval. Replacing such a dependency, upgrading across the move or downgrading it is a dependency change the user approves first.
- Lean to operate: every log line, metric, retained file and background job justifies its cost.

## Scale

Performance items (Runtime, Caching, the efficiency choices in Data access queries and schema, partitioning, pooler adoption, gateways, gRPC, replicas) are sized to the load profile (users, request and message rates, data volume and expected growth, stated or marked assumed): they are worth changing only where that load, or credible near-term growth in it, makes the gap cost something. Correctness and resilience items are weighed by likelihood x impact at any load: instance state another request needs, or singleton work without a lock, where more than one instance runs, sync-over-async, lost or duplicated events, a context shared across threads, writes that bypass interceptors or the outbox, session state lost through a pooler, missing timeouts, unsafe retries, broken probes or shutdown. "Measured" means existing evidence: telemetry (built-in framework and runtime instrumentation counts), a benchmark or load test in the repo, figures from the user, or a cost evident from code shape at a stated (not assumed) load profile, with the arithmetic recorded; without it a measurement-gated item waits, naming the measurement that would decide it. Prefer the framework-native form named (.NET and PostgreSQL shown; other stacks use their equivalents) and the broker, cache, store and flag provider the system already runs; adding a broker, cache or store is an infrastructure change that needs explicit approval, and a new library must justify itself as a dependency. Rate-limit or lock gaps that enable abuse of authentication or other trust-boundary endpoints, and per-request state that can cross requests (a pooled context or a singleton holding tenant or user data), are security or data-exposure defects.

- **Scale-out**: no instance holds state another request needs (sessions, caches that must agree, in-memory queues, local files, timers that assume one instance); that state lives in a shared store. Singleton work (schedulers, non-reentrant jobs) takes a lock released when its owner dies: a lease row with an expiry renewed by the holder, a distributed-cache lease (`SET NX PX` with renewal and an owner check), or a PostgreSQL session advisory lock held on a dedicated direct connection, never through a transaction-mode pooler; not a long-held row lock or open transaction.
- **Request path**: work that must survive a crash or exceeds the request's latency budget leaves the HTTP lifecycle for a queue or background worker. Where a DB change and its event must agree, use a transactional outbox (the existing messaging library's, else a table written in the same transaction and dispatched after), never a distributed transaction or a direct broker publish after commit; consumers are idempotent (an inbox or dedup key), since delivery is at least once. Read replicas, separate read models or CQRS only where measured read load or query shape needs them.
- **Async and concurrency**: no sync-over-async (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`) on request or worker paths. Independent IO in a loop runs concurrently with a bound (`Task.WhenAll` over a bounded batch, `Parallel.ForEachAsync` with `MaxDegreeOfParallelism`, or `System.Threading.Channels` for producer/consumer); ordered or rate-limited calls stay sequential. Cancellation tokens reach every IO call.
- **Runtime**: flag only overrides of the defaults (ASP.NET Core services default to Server GC, and DATAS is on with Server GC from .NET 9): workstation GC in a service or DATAS disabled without a reason, on .NET 8 a memory-bound container where DATAS was not opted in (`<GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode>1</GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode>` or `DOTNET_GCDynamicAdaptationMode=1`), or container CPU and memory limits the runtime cannot see. Allocation work (`ValueTask` for usually-synchronous hot methods, `ArrayPool<T>`/`MemoryPool<T>` for large buffers, source-generated `LoggerMessage`) only on measured hot paths. `System.Text.Json` source generation for hot or trim/AOT-bound serialization; Native AOT is evaluated only for services or workers where startup or memory is the measured cost.
- **Caching**: a two-level cache over the existing distributed cache (L1 only when single-instance) for hot, read-mostly data, with stampede protection, an explicit TTL and an invalidation path per cached entity: `HybridCache` where each instance's L1 may lag an invalidation by its `LocalCacheExpiration`, FusionCache with its backplane where instances must agree promptly. Derived values are computed from stored inputs unless compute cost or query needs justify persisting them, and then have one owner that refreshes them. Binary payloads (MessagePack, Protobuf) for internal cache and queue values only where size or parse cost is measured.
- **Data access** (EF Core, PostgreSQL):
  - Contexts: `AddDbContextPool` where the context holds no per-request state, else no pooling or a pooled factory that resets that state; `IDbContextFactory<T>` for a short-lived context per parallel operation (a context never crosses threads).
  - Queries and writes: `AsNoTracking` and projection to DTOs for reads; `ExecuteUpdateAsync`/`ExecuteDeleteAsync` for set-based writes only where no SaveChanges interceptor, outbox write, concurrency token or domain event depends on the entities, else batched tracked writes; Npgsql binary COPY (`BeginBinaryImport`) or the existing bulk library for high-volume inserts; `AsSplitQuery` where includes multiply rows, with a unique ordering when paged; pagination or `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` streaming for unbounded results, never materialized whole; raw SQL only for measured hot paths; database retries through the provider's execution strategy (`EnableRetryOnFailure`), never an outer Polly retry; with it, every explicit transaction runs inside `CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(...)` (EF Core rejects user-initiated transactions otherwise), with `SaveChangesAsync(acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false)` and `ChangeTracker.AcceptAllChanges()` after commit, or a fresh context per attempt, so a retry rewrites its changes; a non-idempotent unit of work uses `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` with a `verifySucceeded` check, or an equivalent guard, against a commit that succeeded before the retry, or uses a context configured without `EnableRetryOnFailure` with a one-line site reason.
  - Schema and connections: indexes match query predicates (GIN for JSONB containment and key existence, B-tree expression indexes for `->>` equality or ranges, `pg_trgm` GIN indexes for substring `LIKE`/`ILIKE` predicates); partitioning only for entities whose volume needs it; an external pooler (PgBouncer in transaction mode) only where connections across all instances exceed the server's budget, and then nothing relies on session state through it (session advisory locks, `LISTEN`, session `SET`) and Npgsql is set to match (`No Reset On Close=true`; prepared statements disabled unless PgBouncer 1.21+ `max_prepared_statements` is set); transient work tables hard-delete rows on completion or by TTL, and at high volume are time-partitioned with old partitions dropped.
- **Edge and service calls**: public endpoints are rate limited at the edge or app boundary (ASP.NET Core rate limiting middleware, `AddRateLimiter`, token bucket or sliding window, partitioned per client, with the client address taken from forwarded headers only from known proxies; its limits are per instance, which is fine unless a global quota is required). A gateway (YARP) only where several services need shared routing, TLS or auth; gRPC between internal services only where serialization or latency cost is measured; adopting it is an infrastructure change that needs explicit approval.
- **Resilience**: on by default for every call subject to transient faults (network, cloud, IPC), sync or async, in production, tests reaching real services, smoke suites, scripts and CI. Every outbound call has a timeout (HTTP, database command, cache, broker). Use one retry layer, never nested; retry classified transient faults only (connection resets, TLS handshake failures, timeouts, throttling, transient 5xx), bounded with backoff and jitter, honoring Retry-After and logging each retry. Keep the standard HTTP resilience handler's circuit breaker; a script, CI or SDK call needs none beyond the bounded retry; hedging only for idempotent reads with a measured tail-latency problem.
  - Mechanisms: `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` `AddStandardResilienceHandler` with `DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()` for HttpClient (unsafe methods otherwise retry); the database provider execution strategy (`EnableRetryOnFailure`); SDK built-in retry options. Never retry a non-idempotent call unless a server-honored key or the EF Core execution strategy with `verifySucceeded` or an equivalent guard makes it safe; otherwise disable that call's code or SDK retries with a one-line site reason (no owner needed), so a transient fault fails visibly. Add a server-honored key where the server offers one. SDK defaults otherwise stand. For a client with server-honored keys, do not call `DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()`: set one `Retry.ShouldHandle` applying the default transient predicate to safe methods and unsafe requests carrying the key, refusing other unsafe requests. Read the request with `args.Context.GetRequestMessage()`, never `Outcome.Result?.RequestMessage` (the result is null on exceptions). Set the key once per logical operation, above the resilience handler.
  - Tool retry flags and explicitly enabled SDK retries apply only to idempotent requests (including writes made idempotent by a server-honored key). curl does not retry by default; [`curl --retry`](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--retry) does not retry connection resets or TLS handshake failures without `--retry-all-errors`, which retries every error, including permanent ones. Even idempotent GETs use the repo's shared bounded retry helper with curl retries off; add the smallest helper if absent. `Invoke-RestMethod` / `Invoke-WebRequest -MaximumRetryCount` retry any method on 304 and all 400-599, including permanent errors, at fixed `-RetryIntervalSec` intervals; in [PowerShell 7.5.4 source](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/v7.5.4/src/Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Utility/commands/utility/WebCmdlet/Common/WebRequestPSCmdlet.Common.cs#L1165-L1297), only 429 honors numeric Retry-After and connection failures escape the retry loop. These cmdlet flags cannot express the required transient-only backoff/jitter policy: use the shared bounded helper with cmdlet retries off. github-script `retries` defaults to 0; enabling it uses `@octokit/plugin-retry`, which can retry POST and does not guarantee transient-only classification, jitter or Retry-After handling. Enable only for idempotent calls with an adequate policy; otherwise use the shared helper with that SDK retry option off. Tools that already retry downloads (npm, pip, uv, NuGet / `dotnet restore`, cargo) own the one layer: configure their built-in policy, never wrap the command in another retry. One shared bounded helper is allowed only where the standard mechanism cannot express the required policy.
  - Configure standard options when needed: raise a too-short `AttemptTimeout.Timeout` together with `TotalRequestTimeout.Timeout > AttemptTimeout.Timeout` and `CircuitBreaker.SamplingDuration >= 2 * AttemptTimeout.Timeout`, retaining `DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()` except for the keyed-client case above. For a per-client override of a handler inherited from `ConfigureHttpClientDefaults`, use `RemoveAllResilienceHandlers()` immediately followed by `AddStandardResilienceHandler(o => ...)` on that client, retaining that retry predicate and valid coupled timeouts. The inherited handler shares its options name, so `PostConfigure("<client>-standard", ...)` does not reach it. `RemoveAllResilienceHandlers()` is experimental (EXTEXP0001); suppress only that call with a scoped pragma, never project-wide. This exact remove-and-re-add pair and the keyed `Retry.ShouldHandle` above are standard options; neither needs a proven reason. Other removal, disabling or replacement of resilience, or customizing beyond its options (custom Polly pipelines, predicates, delay generators or request markers), needs a proven reason in a one-line site comment: a measured need or a contract the standard cannot express.
  - An intermittent fault on a safely retryable call without resilience is fixed by enabling or restoring the standard mechanism, configured only as needed, with a policy test. A fault persisting through its budget or recurring is a defect to diagnose, never mask with sleeps, catch-and-ignore or blanket reruns. Review flag: unproven `RemoveAllResilienceHandlers`, disabled SDK retries, `MaxRetries = 0`, custom pipelines or, for transient faults, "next run retries". The documented non-idempotent, unkeyed operation is a proven reason to disable its SDK retries. No fix is needed for a transient fault when the code's existing retry, safe for that call, absorbed it, or the call is already correct (retries off with its documented site reason, and no server-honored key is available) and the fault happened once; a recurring one is a defect. A persistent fault (such as an installer hash mismatch) may correctly wait for the next run.
- **Health and control**: separate liveness (process responsive, no dependency checks), readiness (dependencies reachable, warm-up done) and, for slow warm-up, startup endpoints wired to the container platform's probes (Kubernetes, Container Apps); graceful shutdown drains in-flight work. Kill switches only for a component with a recorded failure history or a planned risky rollout, through the existing config or flag provider; each has an owner and stays, while rollout flags carry a removal plan.

## Operations

- **Logging**: structured, consistent templates; correlation/trace ids across requests, jobs and outbound calls. Debug for entry/exit of key operations, Information for decisions and state transitions, Warning for handled-but-unexpected, Error with exception and diagnostic context (ids, operation, inputs that matter; never secrets or PII). An exception is logged once, at the boundary that handles it. Production default Information for app code, Warning for framework noise, levels changeable without redeploy where the stack allows. Traces via OpenTelemetry with W3C context propagated across HTTP, messaging and jobs, and logs carrying the trace id, so one request can be followed end to end; custom spans only around operations that matter for troubleshooting. Metrics stay minimal unless the user asks for more: health checks and alerting on real failures, no per-operation counters by default.
- **Retention**: scheduled eviction for logs, traces and telemetry (defaults by type, about 7-30 days, each with its reason), sampling for high-volume traces, ingestion caps where the provider supports them. Respect retention values set deliberately.
- **Deploy backups**: where deploys leave previous versions (scripts, pipeline steps, slot swaps, release folders, DB backups), keep the latest N, configurable, default and minimum 2. Any pruning change carries these constraints: prune only after a successful deploy and health check; never the running or immediately previous version; log every removal; dry-run mode; the deletion logic and a dry-run result are shown and approved before it runs against any real server.
- **Other lean items**: temp files, caches and old artifacts; TTL for transient tables, queues and blobs; CI artifact and image pruning; unused packages, projects, flags, config keys and dead code; right-sized schedules and polling; framework and health-check log noise.

## Tests

A test gap is worth closing only where a missed regression in the untested code is costly by likelihood x impact (for example core domain rules, money, persistence, published contracts, concurrency, recovery and shutdown paths, stated layer rules, accessibility of primary journeys); coverage percentage is never a target. A test gap, quality defect, or skipped or failing test on a security or data-exposure control path (authentication, authorization, tenant or data isolation, trust-boundary validation, secret and PII handling) is a security defect; where such a test fails or is skipped because the control is wrong, the defect is the control.

- **Inventory**: map each test project to its level, the code it covers, runner and CI trigger (every PR, path-filtered, push, schedule, manual dispatch, or not run in CI); a test project no CI runs is a gap where it covers costly code. Aggregate gaps per project and level (missing coverage, sample locations, the path list), split further where tier or host needs differ, never one per method.
- **Cheapest level that catches it**: each test sits at the lowest level that fails when the behavior breaks:
  - unit for pure logic, domain rules, domain-invariant validation, mapping and boundary values (trust-boundary validators are security paths, above);
  - integration against the real dependency through the repo's existing harness (for example Testcontainers or Aspire; else one the test needs, justified per Quality) for queries, migrations, transactions, concurrency tokens, the outbox, idempotent consumers and anything an in-memory fake would hide;
  - API or contract tests for public endpoints and messages: status codes, error shapes, serialization shape and, where the user or repo states a compatibility obligation, backward compatibility of published contracts (their authorization and validation cases are security paths, above);
  - architecture tests for stated layer or dependency rules that project references do not already enforce (the repo's existing tool; a new one only when requested);
  - E2E or UI only for the few primary user journeys, never as the only coverage of logic a lower level can test, with an automated accessibility check on them where a UI exists (the repo's existing tool, else one justified per Quality).
- **Strategies where they earn their place**: property-based tests for parsers, serializers, money and invariant-heavy logic; snapshot or approval tests for large, stable outputs; resilience tests (injected faults, timeouts, retries, cancellation, shutdown) where a Scale criterion or the code's existing resilience policy requires the behavior.
- **Expensive tiers**: E2E and browser-driven UI tests, load, soak, benchmark, mutation and chaos tests, and integration suites that take more than about 10 minutes (timed, else estimated and marked assumed), run only on manual dispatch (`workflow_dispatch`, never every push or a schedule) when added or first put in CI. Load, soak and benchmark tests are sized to the load profile, and every expensive tier to risk; mutation testing only for core logic where assertion strength is in doubt. Test work leaves the triggers of suites CI already runs alone; a suite no CI runs gets the trigger its tier allows.
- **Quality**: flaky or order-dependent tests, shared mutable state, real clocks, unrecorded random seeds, sleeps, calls to real external services, assertions that cannot fail and tests that mirror the implementation are defects where they hide or fake regressions; so are skipped or quarantined tests with no owner and reason. Tests use the repo's existing frameworks, fixtures, builders and project layout; a new test project only where a level needs its own runner or dependencies, and a new test framework, library or fixture only when requested, except an accessibility checker or real-dependency integration harness a needed test requires, which must justify itself as a dependency (License stability applies).

## Documentation

Code is documented for humans and AI agents alike; gaps are defects, not style. This covers product code; generated code and test projects are out of scope.

- Every class (or the language's equivalent type) and every public or protected member carries API doc comments in the language's standard form (XML docs in C#, JSDoc/TSDoc, docstrings, KDoc and the like): a summary of purpose and behavior, every parameter, the return value, and exceptions callers must handle. In C#, include `<param>` for each parameter, `<returns>`, `<exception>` where thrown, and `<typeparam>` for generics. Private members are documented as needed, where intent or a non-obvious constraint is not clear from the name. Docs state contract and intent, not a restatement of the signature.
- Missing docs are aggregated per project or module (count, sample locations, and the path list), never one per member.
- Every change that adds or changes public API documents it in the same change.
- Where the toolchain can enforce part of it (for example .NET `GenerateDocumentationFile` with missing-doc warnings as errors, which covers visible members only, or the linter's doc rule), a change whose scope is closing a project's doc gaps turns that enforcement on once they are closed, never before; review covers what it cannot enforce.
- A README at the repository root and per deployable project or package: purpose, architecture in brief, how to build, test, configure and run, and where to look next. Agent instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) stay accurate where present.
- Docs that contradict the code are correctness defects, more urgent than missing docs.
